faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Somerville attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night-only scratching in Somerset County often means bats, flying squirrels or raccoons, while daytime running usually points to gray squirrels. Around Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge edge, the cover close to housing means several species are plausible, so call us for an inspection and we will identify the animal before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Somerville porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Somerville with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

Somerville.wildlife_intro:
Somerville gives our crew a Somerset mix shaped by Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge edge and the housing around it. Squirrels, raccoons and moles are steady across Bridgewater, Hillsborough and Franklin's subdivision lawns and canopy streets, Great Swamp-edge towns add bats in older homes, and the Sourlands add groundhogs, black snakes and the county's isolated copperhead colonies — and Somerville is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Somerville and Bound Brook keep older borough stock, Bridgewater and Hillsborough are growth-era subdivisions, Bernardsville holds estate homes in the Somerset Hills, and Franklin mixes farms with dense suburbs. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Somerville; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Somerville jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Bridgewater Township home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Martinsville farmhouse with groundhogs under the barn and raccoons in the chimney, and a new townhouse with starlings in a vent, are both Bridgewater inspections, priced from different checklists entirely. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Bridgewater Township ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Martinsville's wooded streets the morning running enters where the canopy meets the gable, and the repeated subdivisions elsewhere in the township fail at the repeated soffit joint instead. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

Bridgewater Township.wildlife_intro:
Bridgewater is Somerset's suburban crossroads: Martinsville's older, wooded streets in the north, big subdivisions and townhouse complexes around Routes 22 and 287, Chimney Rock's quarry woods, and the Raritan River closing the south side. Squirrels and raccoons work the canopy neighborhoods, groundhogs dig the lots backing onto fields and the river banks, skunks work the lawns, and bats take the attics near the woods. The township's housing spans farmhouse to last-year's construction, and each era brings its own entries.

Newer houses are not exempt — they just fail differently. Vinyl soffits flex and pop at the corners, roof-to-wall joints on additions open as materials settle, and bathroom vents often end in cheap plastic covers that starlings and squirrels push through in a season. Builders leave gaps around garage door corners and utility lines that rats and mice find within the first year. The work on a newer home is detail work: metal where plastic failed, backer rod and sealant at settling joints, and screens behind every vent cover rather than trust in the cover alone. Bridgewater inspections run the era checklists together, farmhouse gaps in the old sections and vent-and-vinyl failures in the new ones, because both stand on the same streets here.

faqs.q: I found a snake in my Hillsborough Township yard — could it be venomous?
faqs.a: Possibly, in this part of New Jersey, which is why identification comes before everything. The northern copperhead (state-Threatened) favors rocky, wooded slopes here, and the timber rattlesnake (state-Endangered) holds on along the ridges; both are left strictly alone and referred to NJ Fish & Wildlife's Venomous Snake Response Team. The Sourlands are one of the copperhead's documented Somerset County homes, rocky woods with sunny ledges, and a banded snake on a Sourland wall or woodpile gets identified before it gets anything else. Most calls turn out to be harmless black rat snakes or garter snakes, which we can catch and release outdoors within 200 meters, as state policy allows.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Hillsborough Township foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Hillsborough's field soils dig soft and deep, and a burrow under a run-in shed or a foundation can run the length of the building before the second entrance shows. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Hillsborough Township.wildlife_intro:
Hillsborough is one of Somerset's biggest townships, running from the Sourland Mountain's rocky woods in the west to subdivisions and farm country in the east, with Neshanic's village and Duke Farms' open land in between. Groundhogs dig the farm and subdivision edges, raccoons take the farmhouses and the colonials alike, bats hold the older attics, skunks are universal, and the Sourlands are copperhead country, rocky, wooded, and one of the snake's few New Jersey strongholds. The township's scale means a call can be a townhouse vent or a forty-acre farmstead.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Hillsborough jobs are scoped to the parcel, because a Sourland-edge farmstead and a subdivision lot need different plans even when the animal is the same.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Franklin Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. Griggstown and Six Mile Run chimneys are canal-era brick and stone, and their spring raccoon litters are a tradition the fitted cap respectfully ends. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

faqs.q: What makes one Franklin Township wildlife job cost more than another?
faqs.a: Access, animal count, and aftermath. A steep roof, a maternity litter that has to be handled as a family, or insulation contaminated wall-to-wall all add time and material. Franklin's range spans a Kingston stone house with a chimney family and a new subdivision colonial with a single vent failure; access and aftermath, not the animal's name, set the difference. The inspection sorts your house into one of those buckets and the written quote shows exactly which items drive the number.

Franklin Township.wildlife_intro:
Franklin Township, the Somerset County one, is a string of villages and subdivisions along the D&R Canal and the Millstone River: Somerset's older streets, Franklin Park, Griggstown's canal village, Six Mile Run's historic district, and Kingston at the south end. The canal corridor is a green highway the length of the township. Raccoons and squirrels work every village, groundhogs dig the field edges and the canal banks, rats appear around the older commercial pockets, and bats hold the attics of the canal-era homes. Housing runs from 1700s stone to this decade's subdivisions.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Franklin's canal-side canopy overhangs a lot of old rooflines, so the limb report here is written with the sealing plan, and canal-corridor houses get it every time.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Bernardsville attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. Estate attics in Bernardsville can hold a colony at one end for years while the house runs normally below, and the droppings map usually shows a roost older than the current owners. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

faqs.q: Once the animals are out of my Bernardsville home, how do I keep them out?
faqs.a: Walk the house the way an animal does: roofline first, then vents, then ground level. Chimney cap, metal-backed vent covers, limbs cut back off the roof, trash in lidded cans, and no pet food or open seed stored in the garage. On a Bernardsville estate the fall list runs long, chimneys, carriage-house vents, pool-house gaps, and the main roof, and it is left as one property checklist rather than a pile of separate notes. We leave you the entry map from your own job — which gaps were sealed and which aging spots to watch — because the houses that stay quiet are checked each fall, not just fixed once.

Bernardsville.wildlife_intro:
Bernardsville is the Somerset Hills in one borough: a small historic village center, then lanes of substantial older homes and estates climbing the wooded hills, with the Scherman Hoffman sanctuary's woods at its edge and Mine Brook running through. The houses are large, old, and complicated, and the lots are deep and wooded. Raccoons and squirrels work the big rooflines, bats hold colonies in the estate attics, groundhogs and skunks take the lawns and outbuildings, and the whole borough sits in some of the most wildlife-rich woods in the county.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Bernardsville attics are large and often finished in sections, so the survey here is compartment by compartment, with photographs for an owner who may not climb up to see any of it.

faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Bound Brook basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Bound Brook's older basements the signs follow the river-side wall, and flood-deposited gaps at the sill are the entries we find most often after high water. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Bound Brook attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. Bound Brook's twins share attic voids in places, and night scratching reported by one household often traces to a raccoon denned over the neighbor's half of the roof. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

Bound Brook.wildlife_intro:
Bound Brook is a small, dense borough in the Raritan River's bend: older singles, twins, and small apartment buildings on a tight grid, a Main Street downtown, and the river and the railroad wrapping the town. Rats work the downtown blocks and the older basements, raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs, squirrels take the eaves along the river-side trees, and bats hold the older attics. The river has flooded this borough memorably, and every flood rearranges ground-level entries and leaves debris lines that animals use as cover.

Storms open houses. Wind lifts shingles and ridge caps, ice works at eave flashing, and a single hard season can hand squirrels and raccoons three new doors into an attic that was tight for a decade. After major weather we check the roofline the way a roofer would — ridge, valleys, eave returns, plumbing stacks — because animal entries and water entries are usually the same gaps. Sealing done alongside sound roof repair lasts; sealing done over rotted, water-softened wood does not, and we will say which situation a house is in before any work is quoted. Bound Brook's river history means ground-level sealing here is checked against the high-water line, and anything the last flood loosened is treated as an open entry until proven otherwise.
